hints: Work out each oxide formula from the oxidation number of the Period 3 element combined with oxide ion, $\text{O}^{2-}$, for example Al is +3 so needs two Al for three O.
Recall how oxide character changes left to right across Period 3, from metal oxides that are basic, through the middle amphoteric oxide, to non-metal oxides that are acidic.
walkthrough:
Build the missing formulae from valency**
Think of oxygen as $\text{O}^{2-}$ every time. Sodium is +1 so you need two Na for one O to give $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$. In the same way aluminium (+3) gives $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$, silicon (+4) gives $\text{SiO}_2$, phosphorus (+5) gives $\text{P}_2\text{O}_5$ which dimerises to $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$, and sulfur (+6) gives $\text{SO}_3$.

Link metal character to acid-base behaviour**
Picture the left side of Period 3 as strongly metallic. $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ is a basic oxide that forms $\text{NaOH}$ with water. In the middle $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ sits on the borderline so it is amphoteric. To the right the elements are non-metallic, so $\text{SiO}_2$, phosphorus oxides and $\text{SO}_3$ all form acids with water and are classed as acidic.

Final answer: Formulae: $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ | $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ | $\text{SiO}_2$ | $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ (allow $\text{P}_2\text{O}_5$, $\text{P}_4\text{O}_6$, $\text{P}_2\text{O}_3$) | $\text{SO}_3$
Acid/base behaviour: basic | amphoteric | acidic | acidic | acidic

hints: Think of what makes $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ special, it can neutralise the opposite extremes of pH.
walkthrough:
Picture a substance with two faces**
An amphoteric hydroxide like $\text{Be(OH)}_2$ can act as a base when it meets an acid, and can also act as an acid when it meets a base. So it reacts with both acids and with bases to form salts.
Final answer: Reacts with both acids and bases (alkalis).

hints: Focus only on the ions that actually change, the $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions stay in solution unchanged.
walkthrough:
Strip the full equation to the real change**
The full reaction is $\text{Mg(OH)}_2 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ appear on both sides as free ions, so they cancel as spectators. What is left is hydroxide neutralising hydrogen ions: $$\text{OH}^{-} + \text{H}^{+} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

hints: Compare the two equations, $\text{Sr} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Sr(OH)}_2 + \text{H}_2$ versus $\text{SrO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Sr(OH)}_2$, and look for the product that gives a visible effect.
walkthrough:
Spot which route makes a gas**
Strontium metal with water gives strontium hydroxide plus hydrogen gas: $$\text{Sr} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Sr(OH)}_2 + \text{H}_2$$ Bubbles of colourless $\text{H}_2$ fizz off. Strontium oxide with water simply dissolves to give the hydroxide with no gas: $$\text{SrO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Sr(OH)}_2$$ So the visible difference is effervescence in reaction 1 only.
Final answer: Reaction 1 effervesces, fizzes or bubbles due to $\text{H}_2$ evolution, reaction 2 shows no effervescence.

hints: Recall that $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is almost insoluble while $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ is much more soluble, so think what happens going down.
walkthrough:
Remember the hydroxide solubility pattern**
Magnesium hydroxide is sparingly soluble and gives only a weakly alkaline suspension, while calcium, strontium and barium hydroxides dissolve more readily to give more strongly alkaline solutions. So solubility increases down the group.
Final answer: Solubility increases down Group 2.

hints: List $p$, $V$ and $T$ in SI units before substituting, $\text{kPa}$ to $\text{Pa}$, $\text{dm}^3$ to $\text{m}^3$, and $^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $\text{K}$.
Use $n = PV/RT$ with $R = 8.31 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{mol}^{-1}$ to find moles of $\text{CO}_2$.
walkthrough:
Convert everything to SI units**
The gas equation needs $\text{Pa}$, $\text{m}^3$ and $\text{K}$. So $p = 5.37 \text{ kPa} = 5.37 \times 10^{3} \text{ Pa}$, $V = 0.500 \text{ dm}^3 = 0.500 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3 = 5.00 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^3$, and $T = 20 + 273 = 293 \text{ K}$.

Apply $n = PV/RT$**
Substitute carefully: $$n = \frac{PV}{RT} = \frac{(5.37 \times 10^{3})(5.00 \times 10^{-4})}{8.31 \times 293}$$ The numerator is $2.685$, the denominator is $2434.83$, giving $n = 1.10 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$ of $\text{CO}_2$.

Final answer: $p = 5.37 \times 10^{3} \text{ Pa}$, $V = 5.00 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^3$, $T = 293 \text{ K}$
$n = PV/RT = (5.37 \times 10^{3} \times 5.00 \times 10^{-4})/(8.31 \times 293) = 1.10 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$

hints: Use the 1:1 mole ratio from $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2 + \text{CO}_2 \rightarrow$ products to link moles of $\text{CO}_2$ to moles of $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$, then multiply by $M_r = 78.0$.
walkthrough:
Scale by the equation then convert to mass**
The equation shows 1 mol $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2$ reacts with 1 mol $\text{CO}_2$, so moles $\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2 = 1.10 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$. With $M_r(\text{Na}_2\text{O}_2) = 2(23.0) + 2(16.0) = 78.0$: $$\text{mass} = n \times M_r = 1.10 \times 10^{-3} \times 78.0 = 0.0860 \text{ g}$$

hints: Count outer electrons, each O brings 6 plus one extra electron for the 1- charge on each O, giving 7 each and 14 in total.
Join the two O atoms with one shared pair to make the single O-O bond, then complete each O to an octet with three lone pairs.
walkthrough:
Count the electrons to share out**
Each oxygen atom has 6 outer electrons, plus one extra for its 1- charge, so 7 each. That is 14 outer electrons in total for $\text{O}_2^{2-}$. Place two O atoms side by side.

Form the single bond and complete octets**
Overlap one dot from one O with one cross from the other to make the O-O bonding pair. Then add three lone pairs to each O so each O is surrounded by 8 electrons (1 bonding pair plus 3 lone pairs). Show the 2- charge outside brackets. Each O then has a full octet and carries a negative charge.
Final answer: Dot-and-cross diagram with O-O single bond (one shared pair, one dot and one cross). Each O has 3 lone pairs, total 14 outer electrons shown, with overall 2- charge.
